The '''Wiener–Araya graph''' is, in [[graph theory]], a graph on 42 vertices with 67 edges. It is [[Hypohamiltonian graph|hypohamiltonian]], which means that
it does not itself have a [[Hamiltonian cycle]] but every graph formed by removing a single vertex from it is [[Hamiltonian graph|Hamiltonian]]. It is also [[Planar graph|planar]].

==History==

Hypohamiltonian graphs were first studied by Sousselier in ''Problèmes plaisants et délectables'' (1963).<ref>{{citation
 |last1= Sousselier |first1= R.
 |title= Problème no. 29: Le cercle des irascibles
 |publisher= Rev. Franç. Rech. Opérationnelle
 | volume = 7 | pages= 405–406 | year= 1963
 }}</ref>
In 1967, Lindgren built an infinite sequence of hypohamiltonian graphs.<ref>{{citation
 | last1  = Lindgren | first1= W. F.
 | title  = An infinite class of hypohamiltonian graphs
 | journal= [[American Mathematical Monthly]]
 | volume = 74 |year= 1967 | issue= 9
 | pages = 1087–1089
 | doi    = 10.2307/2313617 | jstor= 2313617
 | mr = 0224501}}</ref>
He first cited Gaudin, Herz and Rossi,<ref>{{citation
 | last1   = Gaudin | first1 = T.
 | last2   = Herz | first2 = P.
 | last3   = Rossi
 | title   = Solution du problème No. 29
 | journal = Rev. Franç. Rech. Opérationnelle
 | language= fr
 | volume  = 8 | year= 1964 | pages = 214–218}}</ref> then Busacker and Saaty<ref>{{citation
 |last1 = Busacker|first1=R. G.|last2=Saaty|first2=T. L.
 |title = Finite Graphs and Networks
 |year  = 1965}}</ref>
as pioneers on this topic.

From the start, the smallest [[hypohamiltonian graph]] is known: the [[Petersen graph]]. However, the hunt for the smallest [[Planar graph|planar]] [[hypohamiltonian graph]] continues. This question was first raised by [[Václav Chvátal]] in 1973.<ref>{{citation
 | last1   =Chvátal | first1 = V. | authorlink = Václav Chvátal
 | title   = Flip-flops in hypo-Hamiltonian graphs
 | journal = [[Canadian Mathematical Bulletin]]
 | volume  = 16 | year= 1973 | pages = 33–41 | mr = 0371722 | doi=10.4153/cmb-1973-008-9 | doi-access=free}}</ref>
The first candidate answer was provided in 1976 by [[Carsten Thomassen (mathematician)|Carsten Thomassen]], who exhibited a 105-vertices construction, the [[105-Thomassen graph]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Thomassen | first = Carsten | authorlink = Carsten Thomassen (mathematician)
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]
 | mr = 0422086
 | pages = 377–389
 | title = Planar and infinite hypohamiltonian and hypotraceable graphs
 | volume = 14
 | year = 1976
 | doi=10.1016/0012-365x(76)90071-6| doi-access = 
 }}</ref>
In 1979, Hatzel improved this result with a [[Planar graph|planar]] [[hypohamiltonian graph]] on 57 vertices : the [[Hatzel graph]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Hatzel | first = Wolfgang
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01424541 | doi-access=
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[Mathematische Annalen]]
 | language = German
 | mr = 548801
 | pages = 213–216
 | title = Ein planarer hypohamiltonscher Graph mit 57 Knoten
 | volume = 243
 | year = 1979| s2cid = 121794449
 }}</ref>
This bound  was lowered in 2007 by the [[48-Zamfirescu graph]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Zamfirescu | first1 = Carol T.
 | last2 = Zamfirescu | first2 = Tudor I.
 | doi = 10.1002/jgt.20241
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Journal of Graph Theory]]
 | mr = 2336805
 | pages = 338–342
 | title = A planar hypohamiltonian graph with 48 vertices
 | volume = 55
 | year = 2007| s2cid = 260477281
 }}</ref>

In 2009, a graph built by Gábor Wiener and Makoto Araya became (with its 42 vertices) the smallest [[Planar graph|planar]] [[hypohamiltonian graph]] known.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Wiener | first1 = Gábor
 | last2 = Araya | first2 = Makoto
 | title = The ultimate question 
 | arxiv = 0904.3012
 | date = April 20, 2009| bibcode = 2009arXiv0904.3012W}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Wiener | first1 = Gábor
 | last2 = Araya | first2 = Makoto
 | doi = 10.1002/jgt.20513
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Journal of Graph Theory]]
 | mr = 2809563
 | pages = 55–68
 | title = On planar hypohamiltonian graphs
 | volume = 67
 | year = 2011| s2cid = 5340663
 }}.</ref>
In their paper, Wiener and Araya conjectured their graph to be optimal arguing that its order ([[42 (number)|42]]) appears to be the
[[Phrases from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy#Answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything (42)|answer to The Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything]] from [[The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy]], a [[Douglas Adams]] novel. However, subsequently, smaller planar hypohamiltonian graphs have been discovered.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Jooyandeh | first1 = Mohammadreza
 | last2 = McKay | first2 = Brendan D. | author2-link = Brendan McKay (mathematician)
 | last3 = Östergård | first3 = Patric R. J.
 | last4 = Pettersson | first4 = Ville H.
 | last5 = Zamfirescu | first5 = Carol T.
 | doi = 10.1002/jgt.22015
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Journal of Graph Theory]]
 | mr = 3601121
 | pages = 121–133
 | title = Planar hypohamiltonian graphs on 40 vertices
 | volume = 84
 | year = 2017| s2cid = 5535167
 | arxiv = 1302.2698
 }}</ref>
